chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
title: A white fan says "you're not like the others" in San Antonio
summary: A white man tells the Armstrong band members they are different from "niggers" in town, and Budd reflects on where the band's members came from.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: And one of the places -- I never will forget -- we went to San Antonio, Texas, and we played at a roadhouse out there. Well, it wasn't quite called roadhouses then. I think they were called like caberets, but it was still out -- out on the outskirts of town. And we were all staying, naturally, in the black neighborhood, so we were all sitting out on the porch one day, talking, and you know, just killing time, and a white fellow walked up to us and he says, "I found out where you guys live. I just wanted to come and talk with you and say hello. Welcome you to San Antonio, Texas. I heard the band last night, but I didn't get a chance to say anything to you, so you guys were real great."

He says, "But you don't mind if I say something, do you?" So we says, "No, what do you want to say?" He say, "Well, you know one thing? In talking with you fellows," he said, "You're not niggers." He says, "You're different from what we've got down here." He says, "These are niggers down here. They're not as intelligent as you guys are." "You know, you are not niggers." You know, well.

First we flinched a little bit, but then we realized that the guy was sincere. He thought he was saying something. He didn't know, darn near down to everybody, and the band was from the south, actually. Teddy Wilson from Austin, Texas. My brother and I.
And I think the only New York guys in the band was the Oldham brothers.
I mean Chicago guys. Because Mike McKendrick was from Indiana.
And Yank Porter. I don't know where he was from, but we got him out of New York.
